titre: The Ambassador Whom Bailiffs Dared to Arrest
accroche: In 1708 in London, bailiffs arrest the Russian ambassador over an unpaid debt. The incident produces the first law codifying diplomatic immunity.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1708, the Russian ambassador Andrey Matveyev settled in London to try to persuade Queen Anne to mediate between Sweden and Russia, and not to recognize Stanisław Leszczyński as king of Poland. Just before leaving England, he is arrested by bailiffs acting on behalf of creditors. They hold him in a debtors' lockup, where he remains until fifty pounds are paid. The account describes them as “a Brutal sort of People.”

## An immunity that was still only a custom

At this date, no English law guarantees the immunity of ambassadors: it falls under custom between sovereigns, not under a written rule that neighborhood bailiffs are expected to know. Matveyev's arrest demonstrates it brutally: customary international law protects an ambassador only if those who arrest him know of it and respect it.

Parliament and the queen then offer their apologies, but that is not enough: the diplomatic corps in London is loudly indignant over the incident. To appease Peter the Great, Parliament passes the Diplomatic Privileges Act (7 Ann. c. 12), whose reference entry gives a commencement date of November 16, 1708 (the start of the parliamentary session) and royal assent on April 21, 1709. It is the first law to guarantee diplomatic immunity in writing in England. It voids any civil suit brought against ambassadors and their servants, and declares that whoever brings or carries one out will be deemed a “violator of the law of nations.” It presents itself as a declaratory law of the common law, a presentation that jurists later disputed.

## What the law changes, and what it does not

The 1708 law presents immunity as already existing, and puts it in writing. That difference matters: a merely customary principle depends on who knows it and is willing to apply it; a codified principle binds even a bailiff who has never heard of the law of nations. Its sections 1 and 2 are repealed in 1867 by a statute law revision act, its section 6 in 1887 by another, and the whole by the Diplomatic Privileges Act 1964, on October 1, 1964. Codifying a custom is never a final destination, only one more stage.

repere.texte: The bailiffs hold the Russian ambassador until fifty pounds are paid. The law that results, the first to guarantee diplomatic immunity in writing, bears the date of November 16, 1708 (start of session) and receives royal assent on April 21, 1709.
repere.source: Diplomatic Privileges Act 1708 (7 Ann. c. 12) and biography of Andrey Matveyev, Wikipedia entries

carte.punch: Bailiffs arrest an ambassador for debt; England invents written immunity.
carte.idee: In 1708, London bailiffs arrest the Russian ambassador for debt. Despite apologies from Parliament and the queen, the diplomatic corps is indignant, and Parliament passes the first law guaranteeing ambassadors' immunity in writing.

quiz.question: Before the 1708 law, what was an ambassador's protection in England based on?
choix: Diplomatic custom, with no statute imposing it
A bilateral treaty signed between England and each foreign power
A protection granted only to ambassadors residing in a royal palace
Canon law, applied to ambassadors as to members of the clergy
quiz.explication: Before 1708, no English law guarantees the immunity of ambassadors: it falls under custom, and therefore depends on those who apply it. Matveyev's arrest by bailiffs shows the limit of a merely customary protection, and Parliament then passes a text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was Ambassador Andrey Matveyev in London in 1708?
choix: To try to persuade Queen Anne to mediate between Russia and Sweden
To negotiate a fur trade treaty between Russia and England
To represent Russia at Queen Anne's coronation
To buy warships on behalf of Peter the Great
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Matveyev settled in London to persuade Queen Anne to mediate between Sweden and Russia, and not to recognize Leszczyński as king of Poland.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did the bailiffs arrest Matveyev?
choix: For a traffic offense committed with his carriage
At the request of creditors, over debts
On the direct order of Parliament, which suspected him of espionage
For refusing to pay a customs duty on his diplomatic baggage
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The bailiffs were acting on behalf of the ambassador's creditors: he was held in a debtors' lockup until fifty pounds were paid.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does the Diplomatic Privileges Act of 1708 declare about anyone who would sue an ambassador in civil court?
choix: That he becomes liable to a fine equal to the debt claimed
That he must obtain prior royal authorization before any suit
That he commits a separate criminal offense, tried by Parliament
That he becomes a “violator of the law of nations”
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The law voids any civil suit against an ambassador or his servants, and deems whoever brought or carried one out a “violator of the law of nations.”
